source.repro: node --expose-gc plugins/comparative-adapters/benches/pafLineParse.bench.ts --rounds=30 for the minimap2 row, and the same with --only=big and PAF_BENCH_PATH set for the two PIF rows — the bench header carries the recipe that cuts those fixtures out of hs1ToMm39.over.chain.pif.gz. One process per fixture. Min of rounds; the ranges span every sample whose control landed in 0.98-1.05, and a sample outside that measured nothing and is not in them. Six samples on the minimap2 row, five on each PIF row.
source.notes:
One line of text to one SyntenyFeature — the read path of both in-memory PAF adapters and both indexed PIF adapters. Two changes landed together and the bench reads them apart: `parsePAFLine` walking tab offsets instead of `line.split('\t')`, and the two feature builders dropping a `...rest` spread from the middle of their data-object literal.

THE RANGES ARE WIDE BECAUSE THE MACHINE WAS BUSY — load average ~7 of 16 cores from other agents, for the whole session. They are the spread actually observed rather than a tightened quote, so a re-run on a quiet box should land inside them and probably near the top. What did not move: both changes helped on every sample, and `both` beat `offsets` on every sample but one (the coarse row where they crossed at 1.58/1.55).

The feature build is the larger of the two changes, which is the surprise — the cost model above, and ADR-039's note about it, are both written about the parse. Reading the two columns against each other per sample, the parse change is 1.10-1.41x and the spread removal is worth another 1.4-1.8x on top of it. The parse measured on its own, with no feature built at all, is 1.4-2.0x.

Row count is this harness's ceiling and it is low: past ~4,000 rows per arm the control falls to 0.63-0.79x while the candidate arms keep reporting plausible ratios. See BENCHMARKING.md; the bench warns above 6,000.
